title: The Terror of Taking Yourself Too Seriously
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article distinguishes between taking one's work seriously — a genuine asset in achieving results — and letting that seriousness metastasize into self-importance. It describes the pattern of "imperial" leaders who view their priorities as inherently more important than others', insert themselves into everyone's work, and grow angry when contradicted. The piece argues this self-inflation makes leaders poor listeners and insufferable colleagues, and closes with G.K. Chesterton's line about angels flying because they take themselves lightly.
points: Taking one's work seriously is valuable; taking oneself too seriously becomes a liability.
"Imperial" leaders view their own priorities as more important than others' and insert themselves into everyone's work.
This self-importance makes leaders poor listeners who talk incessantly about themselves and expect confirmation of their greatness.
The line between serious work and self-seriousness can blur but should be maintained deliberately.
The article closes with G.K. Chesterton's observation that angels can fly because they take themselves lightly.
quotes: A serious and weighty approach to results is a tremendous asset when it is applied to the tasks at hand. But if that seriousness is allowed to corrupt the identity and self-image of the leader, it then becomes a huge liability.
Any time a leader begins to view themselves as an indispensable source of insight and wisdom, they stand on the cliff edge of self-worship.
Not surprisingly, they become frustrated and angry when people disagree with them or resist their views.
There is simply no good reason for you to allow the pursuit of success to color the way you see yourself.
As the English philosopher and critic G.K. Chesterton so aptly stated, “Angels can fly because they take themselves lightly.
